migrationNotes: Spine: sit in a car at the lights and watch the speedometer. Name the rate at which the reading changes, work it out from two readings, then follow its sign through a slowing cart, a leftward cart and a cart that stops for an instant.

Left out of the lesson (still in the course): phys-changing-velocity-2 (the same numbers as the worked example) and -rate. The sums are covered by -1 and the worked example. -6 was reworded so that it no longer needs the velocity–time graph, which this lesson does not draw.

lesson.title: Changing velocity

lead.text: Return to the traffic lights. Suppose the car gains 3 metres per second of velocity during every second that passes. At the start it is at rest. After 1 s the needle reads 3 m/s, after 2 s it reads 6 m/s and after 3 s it reads 9 m/s. The reading rises by the same amount each second, and that amount is the number we are after.

How quickly the velocity changes is called acceleration. For this car it is 3 metres per second, every second, which is written 3 m/s². The unit tells the story: a velocity in m/s changes, and it does so over a stretch of seconds, so seconds appear twice. A larger acceleration means the velocity changes faster. A car with an acceleration of 1 m/s² would need 9 s to reach the 9 m/s that ours reaches in 3.

afterFigure.text: Acceleration answers the question that the speedometer leaves open. Velocity tells you how the position is changing right now. Acceleration tells you how that velocity is changing right now. The next screens turn that idea into a sum.

lead.text: A different car is already rolling when the driver presses the accelerator.

Often you are given two velocities and the time between them, and the acceleration has to be found. Take the change in velocity, which is the finishing velocity minus the starting one, and divide it by the time the change took.

Say a cyclist speeds up from 4 m/s to 16 m/s in 3 s. The change in velocity is 16 − 4 = 12 m/s, spread over 3 s, so the acceleration is 12 ÷ 3 = 4 m/s². This is an average, like the average velocity we found earlier. The velocity might not have changed at an even rate, and the sum gives only the overall rate for the stretch.

afterFigure.text: The sum works for any pair of velocities, so it also works when they are negative. That matters in a moment, because a negative velocity is just motion in the negative direction. First, try the sum on a case where everything is positive.

lead.text: A cart's velocity climbs steadily while a stopwatch runs.

reveal.text: You divided the change in velocity by the time. Equal time steps add equal velocity changes when the acceleration is constant.

lead.text: Velocities have signs, so accelerations do too. The sum uses final minus initial, and it gives the right sign automatically. A cart that slows from 8 m/s to 2 m/s in 3 s changes by 2 − 8 = −6 m/s, so its acceleration is −6 ÷ 3 = −2 m/s². The negative sign is there because the velocity went down.

Now send a cart the other way. A cart that goes from −1 m/s to −9 m/s in 4 s changes by −9 − (−1) = −8 m/s, which gives −8 ÷ 4 = −2 m/s² as well. This time the cart is speeding up, because it moves left faster and faster. The same acceleration slowed the first cart and sped up the second.

afterFigure.text: To tell which one is happening, compare the signs of the velocity and the acceleration. When they match, the acceleration pushes the same way as the motion and the cart speeds up. When they differ, the acceleration works against the motion and the cart slows down. A minus sign on its own does not say whether something is speeding up.

cases.label: Faster to the left: −1 m/s to −9 m/s

steps.headline: A cart moving left goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s in 3 s. Find its acceleration.

workedSteps.text: The change in velocity is final minus initial. Subtracting −8 adds 8.
The velocity went up towards zero, so the change is positive.

lead.text: Compare the directions of the velocity and the acceleration, rather than reading anything into a minus sign.

Two mix-ups are worth clearing away. The first is a cart that holds 5 m/s for 3 s. Its velocity does not change, so the change in velocity is 0 and the acceleration is 0 ÷ 3 = 0 m/s². The cart is moving the whole time, yet its acceleration is zero, because acceleration measures how the velocity changes and says nothing about how large the velocity is.

The second is the reverse. Roll a cart up a gentle slope. It slows, stops for an instant at the top and rolls back down. Its velocity passes through +2, +1, 0, −1 and −2 m/s, one step every second, so it changes by −1 m/s each second the whole way. At the instant of stopping, its velocity is zero. Its acceleration is still −1 m/s², because the velocity is in the middle of changing.

afterFigure.text: Velocity and acceleration are separate quantities, and either can be zero while the other is not. The way to find acceleration is the same each time: the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

cases.label: Up the slope and back: 2 m/s to −2 m/s

lead.text: A cart rolls along a flat track without speeding up or slowing down.

reveal.text: Velocity did not change, so acceleration is zero, yet the position keeps changing.

lesson.orientation: Read acceleration as a signed change in velocity per second.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Sit in the front passenger seat of a car at the traffic lights and watch the speedometer. The light turns green and the driver sets off. The needle swings round: first 0, then 3 metres per second, then 6, then 9. It never stays still, because the car's velocity is changing all the time.

Until now every trip we described had a velocity that stayed fixed along each stretch, so one number was enough. The car in the queue needs two. One says how fast it is going, and the other says how quickly that is changing. You feel the second one in your back as the seat pushes you forwards. A gentle start and a hard start can reach the same velocity and feel completely different, because the velocity changed at different rates.
That rate is the subject of this lesson. We'll give it a name and learn to work it out from a trip.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find acceleration from a change in velocity and read its sign.

recap.keyIdea: Acceleration is the change in velocity over the time it takes. Its sign comes from final minus initial velocity, and whether something speeds up or slows down depends on how that sign compares with the velocity's.

blocks.text: You found that a car at 10 m/s gaining 3 m/s each second reaches 22 m/s after 4 s. You also saw that a cart going from −8 to −2 m/s has a positive acceleration while it slows, and that a steady velocity means zero acceleration.

recap.nextHook: We can now describe how velocity changes. Next we use that to predict how fast a cart will be going, and where it will be, some seconds from now.

questions.prompt: A cart changes velocity from 2 m/s to 10 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Find the signed change in velocity.
Divide that change by the elapsed time.
Subtract initial from final velocity, then divide by duration.
questions.onCorrect: 2 m/s². Acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time it took.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in velocity. Divide by the time to get a rate.
That divides the final velocity by the time. Use the change in velocity.

questions.prompt: Velocity changes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s over 3 s. What is the average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: Subtract the initial negative velocity carefully.
The velocity moves toward zero.
Calculate (−2 − (−8))/3.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The velocity change is −2 − (−8) = +6 m/s. Dividing by 3 s gives +2 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². Velocity rose from −8 to −2, so acceleration is positive even though the cart is slowing.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart is slowing, but acceleration is final minus initial velocity. That change is positive.
That adds the two velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A cart has negative velocity and negative acceleration. What happens to its speed while those signs remain?
hints: Compare the directions, rather than interpreting a minus sign as braking.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Velocity and acceleration both point left, so the magnitude of velocity increases.

questions.onCorrect: Its speed increases. Velocity and acceleration point the same way, so the cart speeds up.

misconceptions.feedback: A minus sign alone does not mean slowing down. Compare the directions of velocity and acceleration.
Nothing here makes the velocity zero. It only grows in the direction it already points.

questions.prompt: A cart keeps a velocity of 6 m/s for 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Acceleration depends on a change in velocity.
Compare the initial and final velocities.
Calculate (6 − 6)/4.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: There is no velocity change: (6 − 6)/4 = 0 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: 0 m/s². Velocity did not change, so there is no acceleration, though the cart keeps moving.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the velocity. Acceleration is how much the velocity changes.
That divides the velocity by the time. Acceleration needs a change in velocity.

questions.prompt: A robot's velocity changes from 9 m/s to −3 m/s in 4 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: The final velocity points opposite to the initial velocity.
Keep signs when subtracting.
Divide the negative velocity change by elapsed time.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The change is −3 − 9 = −12 m/s. Acceleration is −12/4 = −3 m/s².

questions.onCorrect: −3 m/s². The velocity change is final minus initial, and it is negative because the robot reverses.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the velocity falls. The sign has to show that.
That adds the velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.

questions.prompt: A cart's velocity changes steadily from positive to negative, passing through zero on the way. At the instant its velocity is zero, which description is possible?
hints: Think of a cart that rolls up a slope and stops for an instant before it rolls back.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The graph's value is zero at the crossing, while its slope remains nonzero.

choices.label: Zero velocity must mean zero acceleration

questions.onCorrect: Zero velocity with nonzero acceleration. A velocity can pass through zero while it is still changing.

misconceptions.feedback: Velocity and acceleration are separate quantities. A cart can pass through zero velocity while its velocity is still changing.
The velocity changes steadily, so the acceleration has one value throughout. It does not switch off at zero.

questions.prompt: A car is rolling at 10 m/s. Each second it picks up another 3 m/s. How fast is it going after 4 s, in m/s?
hints: How much does the speed gain in 4 seconds?
Four lots of 3 m/s.
Add the gain to the 10 m/s start.
questions.onCorrect: 22 m/s. A steady gain per second is the idea of acceleration: velocity changing at a steady rate.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds only the first second's gain. The car gains 3 m/s every second.
That adds only one second's gain. Count all four seconds.

questions.prompt: A cart's velocity goes from 3 m/s to 15 m/s in 4 s. What is its average acceleration in m/s²?
hints: How much did the velocity change?
Divide that change by the time it took.
Take 3 away from 15, then share it over 4 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: 3 m/s². Acceleration is change in velocity per second.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the change in velocity. Divide it by the time as well.
That uses the final velocity alone. Subtract the starting velocity first.

questions.prompt: Why is the acceleration positive when the cart goes from −8 m/s to −2 m/s?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.

choices.label: Its velocity increases, from −8 up to −2.
Velocity and acceleration always have the same sign.

questions.onCorrect: Acceleration is final minus initial velocity. Here that is +6, even though the cart is slowing.

misconceptions.feedback: Its speed falls from 8 m/s to 2 m/s. The acceleration is positive for another reason.
They have opposite signs whenever something slows down. Look at the change in velocity.

questions.prompt: A cart moving at −10 m/s slows to −4 m/s in 3 s. Find its average acceleration in m/s².
hints: Final velocity minus initial velocity.
Subtracting a negative number adds its size.
Divide the change by 3 seconds.
questions.onCorrect: +2 m/s². The velocity rises towards zero, so the acceleration is positive while the cart slows.

misconceptions.feedback: The cart is slowing, but acceleration is the change in velocity. That change is positive.
That adds the two velocities. Subtract the initial from the final.
